name: LoCoMo: Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents
venue: ACL 2024 (Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Volume 1: Long Papers; ACL Anthology 2024.acl-long.747, Bangkok, Thailand, August 2024). Preprint arXiv:2402.17753 (cs.CL), submitted 27 Feb 2024.
authors_affiliation: Adyasha Maharana (University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill); Dong-Ho Lee (University of Southern California); Sergey Tulyakov (Snap Inc.); Mohit Bansal (UNC Chapel Hill, equal advising); Francesco Barbieri (Snap Inc., equal advising); Yuwei Fang (Snap Inc., equal advising). Primary affiliations: UNC Chapel Hill, USC, and Snap Inc.
maintained_repo_url: https://github.com/snap-research/locomo (official Snap Research repo hosting the LoCoMo dataset data/locomo10.json and evaluation scripts; project page https://snap-research.github.io/locomo/). No live leaderboard is maintained by the authors, though LoCoMo has been widely adopted as a standard long-term-memory benchmark by later systems (e.g. Mem0, MemGPT, A-MEM, Memory-R1).
task_domain: memory / QA (very long-term conversational memory benchmark): evaluates an LLM agent's long-term memory over multi-session open-domain dialogues via three tasks: question answering, event-graph summarization, and multi-modal dialogue generation. Touches retrieval (RAG over conversation history) and temporal/causal reasoning.
problem_setting: Offline benchmark for measuring long-term memory of LLM agents over very long, multi-session, multi-modal open-domain dialogues. The authors first build a machine-human GENERATIVE PIPELINE: two LLM-based generative agents (each a gpt-3.5-turbo agent with a unique persona, a temporal event graph of causally-linked life events, and a Park et al. 2023 generative-agent memory/reflection module plus image-sharing/image-reaction behaviors) converse over up to 35 sessions; human annotators then verify and edit ~15% of turns and remove/substitute ~19% of images for long-range consistency and grounding to the event graphs. The resulting LoCoMo dataset (originally 50 conversations on arXiv v1; the released benchmark is a curated 10-conversation subset locomo10.json with the longest, highest-quality conversations) averages ~300 turns, ~9.2K tokens, and ~19 sessions per conversation. The EVALUATION setting is then offline, single-turn-at-a-time inference over a frozen, fully-observed conversation: given the (truncated, full, or retrieved) conversation history, a model must (a) answer annotated questions in five reasoning categories (single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, open-domain knowledge, adversarial), (b) summarize each speaker's event graph, and (c) generate the next multi-modal dialogue turn. It compares three model classes: short-context base LLMs (history truncated), long-context LLMs, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) over a database of dialogs / observations / session summaries. Human upper-bound performance is reported for QA. Supervision: QA/event annotations are human-curated; for multimodal dialogue, three MiniGPT-5 variants are trained on 50 auto-generated (un-filtered) conversations.
what_is_retrieved: For the RAG QA setting, retrieved units are past CONVERSATION CONTENT in one of three database forms: (a) raw dialog turns (utterances), (b) observations (atomic assertions/facts about each speaker's life and persona extracted per turn), or (c) session-level summaries. The retrieved context is then fed to a reader LLM to answer the question. (Note: retrieval also appears inside the data-GENERATION pipeline, where each agent retrieves relevant observations from its long-term memory to condition the next response; but the headline benchmark evaluates RAG over dialog history at inference.)
retrieval_grounding: GROWING/episodic memory of the conversation itself, treated as a per-conversation static store at evaluation time. The retrievable store is the agent's/conversation's own dialogue history (and derived observations/summaries), i.e. an episodic conversational memory rather than an external static KB/doc corpus or API library. Within a single evaluation it is fixed (the full conversation is known); conceptually it represents the growing memory of a long-running dialogue.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Fixed top-k retrieval objective: RAG retrieves the top-k items (dialogs/observations/summaries) by similarity for a query, with k swept over {5,10,25,50} for dialog/observation and {2,5,10} for summary. The paper reports Recall@k of the gold answer-containing context. The key empirical finding is that more is not better: QA F1 with observations peaks at top-5 and DEGRADES as k grows (signal-to-noise ratio), so although high k yields high recall, a smaller precision-oriented k gives better answers; the objective is effectively precision-driven top-k rather than recovering a complete minimal set.
retrieval_unit: Variable by database: (a) a single dialog turn/utterance, (b) a single observation = an atomic assertion (fact) about a speaker derived from one turn, or (c) a session-level summary. Granularity ranges from snippet/single-turn (dialog), to distilled fact (observation), to summary (session). The most effective unit reported is the observation.
index_source: Growing/episodic conversational memory built per conversation: the retrievable store is derived from the LoCoMo dialogue itself. Observations and session summaries are generated offline with gpt-3.5-turbo from the conversation (and released with the dataset). At evaluation each conversation's store is fixed/fully observed; it is not a cross-corpus external KB and is not induced from the model's own test-time trajectories.
index_structure_topology: Flat vector index: each database (dialogs, observations, or session summaries) is embedded and retrieved by dense similarity (DRAGON), with no graph or hierarchical topology over the retrievable units. (The dataset itself is grounded on per-speaker temporal EVENT GRAPHS with causal links, but those event graphs are ground-truth annotations / generation scaffolding, not the retrieval index used by the RAG reader.)
retriever_type: Dense retriever: DRAGON (Lin et al., 2023, 'How to train your DRAGON: Diverse augmentation towards generalizable dense retrieval') is used as the retriever, with gpt-3.5-turbo-16k as the reader. Off-the-shelf dense bi-encoder retrieval; no BM25/learned-for-task/generative retriever.
retriever_learning_signal: None for the benchmark task (off-the-shelf): DRAGON is used as a pre-trained generalizable dense retriever without task-specific fine-tuning on LoCoMo. The paper explicitly notes a limitation that retrieval models are trained on generic semantic-similarity tasks rather than on dialogue, which hurts retrieval of co-referential/anaphoric dialogue content; no contrastive/LM-feedback/RL retraining of the retriever is performed.
query_construction: Raw question as query: in the QA RAG setting the question is used (as-is) to retrieve relevant dialogs/observations/summaries from the conversation database; there is no query decomposition, expansion, or thought-conditioning at inference. (In the separate data-generation pipeline, the agent retrieves observations relevant to the ongoing dialogue context to condition its next response.)
query_granularity: Task/turn-level: one retrieval per QA question (one-shot per query). Not step-decomposed or two-level. In the generative pipeline retrieval is per dialogue turn/session.
when_to_retrieve: One-shot: a single retrieval is issued per QA question before the reader answers. No iterative/active/adaptive re-retrieval loop is used in the benchmark.
retrieval_trigger_signal: Fixed schedule: retrieval is always performed once per QA question (RAG condition), with a preset top-k. There is no confidence/uncertainty/learned-router/reflection-token trigger; whether to retrieve is determined by the experimental condition (Base vs Long-context vs RAG), not by the model at runtime.
reranking: None: top-k items are taken directly from the DRAGON dense-similarity ranking and fed to the reader; no cross-encoder, RRF, or hierarchy-aware reranking stage is applied.
retrieved_context_refinement: Pre-indexing transformation rather than post-retrieval refinement: the main lever is the FORM of the retrievable unit (raw dialog vs distilled observations vs session summaries). Converting dialogs into observations (atomic assertions) acts as a distillation/denoising step that improves QA. The paper notes reducing top-k improves signal-to-noise ratio (implicit truncation), but there is no explicit post-retrieval reranking, distractor-filtering, or compression module at inference.
how_retrieved_used: Prompt augmentation: the top-k retrieved dialogs/observations/summaries are concatenated into the reader LLM's (gpt-3.5-turbo-16k) context to answer the question (QA) or, for multimodal generation, retrieved observations are supplied as additional training/inference context to MiniGPT-5. No skill reuse, case adaptation, or latent-token injection.
planning_integration: Retrieve-then-read (no planning): for QA, a single retrieval step precedes a single answer generation; there is no multi-step planning, tree search, or interleaved act/observe loop in the benchmark evaluation. (The generative pipeline embeds retrieval inside a reflect-and-respond agent loop, but that is for data creation, not the evaluated task.)
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: Per-answer: retrieval happens once and the model produces the answer; retrieval is not interleaved per CoT step, per sentence, or per tool call.
retrieved_item_representation: Surface forms: (a) raw dialog turns (verbatim utterances with speaker), (b) observations rendered as natural-language atomic assertions/facts about a speaker, or (c) free-text session summaries. Injected as text into the reader context; no executable program, structured note, or latent-soft tokens.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Spans the abstraction axis: raw dialogue turn (lowest), distilled atomic fact/assertion (observation, mid), and session summary (higher). The observation form (distilled per-speaker assertions) is the most effective for QA, indicating mid-level distillation beats both raw turns (noisy) and summaries (lossy).
noise_robustness_mechanism: Implicit, via unit choice and small k: distilling dialogs into observations (assertions) and using a small top-k improves the signal-to-noise ratio of retrieved context. The paper shows performance DEGRADES with more retrieved observations and that improper retrieved context can hurt (especially open-domain knowledge questions), but there is no dedicated relevance-evaluator, self-reflection, or distractor-aware-training mechanism; robustness is a measured weakness rather than an engineered defense.
memory_type: episodic (conversational): the evaluated 'memory' is the agent's episodic memory of the prior multi-session conversation. The data-generation agents additionally use a reflection-based long-term memory of observations plus short-term session summaries (Park et al. 2023 generative-agent architecture). No skill-library/workflow/procedural/latent memory.
write_back: true (in the generative pipeline; N/A for the benchmark-eval RAG): during data generation, each agent writes per-turn observations to long-term memory and per-session summaries to short-term memory after each session, then retrieves them to condition future responses. In the benchmark EVALUATION the conversation store is precomputed and frozen, so no test-time write-back occurs while answering questions.
online_growth: Mixed: during conversation GENERATION the memory grows turn-by-turn / session-by-session as the dialogue proceeds. During benchmark EVALUATION the per-conversation store (dialogs/observations/summaries) is fixed and fully observed; it does not grow from the reader's own outputs.
write_back_trigger: Per-turn and per-session (generation pipeline): a single dialogue turn is converted into an observation and stored in long-term memory each turn, and a session summary is produced and stored after each session. There is no success/failure-conditioned or reflective-critique write-back; for the evaluated QA/summarization tasks the trigger is effectively 'never' (precomputed store).
failure_experience_usage: N/A / none: the memory stores observations/summaries of the conversation, not success-vs-failure experiences; no negative/failed experiences are stored or contrastively retrieved. (The benchmark instead probes failure indirectly via adversarial questions that should be answered 'unanswerable'.)
memory_evolution_update: Append-with-running-summarization (generation pipeline): observations are appended to long-term memory per turn (append-only); the session summary w_k is produced by conditioning on the latest session history h_k and the previous summary w_{k-1}, i.e. an incrementally-refined running summary. Stored observations are not later mutated/dedup-merged/pruned. For the benchmark eval, the store is static (no evolution).
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No: retrieval/selection is fixed dense top-k similarity (DRAGON), not an RL- or value-learned retrieval policy.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: No: each conversation has its own private per-speaker/per-conversation memory; there is no cross-agent or cross-framework shared retrievable memory. (Two agents converse during generation, but each maintains its own private memory.)
benchmarks: LoCoMo (introduced by this paper): the released benchmark (data/locomo10.json) contains 10 very long-term conversations (a curated subset of the original 50 on arXiv v1), each ~300 turns, ~9.2K tokens, up to 35 sessions (avg ~19.3 sessions, ~304.9 turns, ~9,209.2 tokens per conversation), spanning a few months, multi-modal (image-sharing). Three evaluation tasks: (1) Question Answering with 5 reasoning categories (single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, open-domain, adversarial), F1; (2) Event-graph Summarization, FactScore precision/recall/F1 + ROUGE; (3) Multi-modal Dialogue Generation, MM-Relevance + NLG metrics. Compared in Table 1 against MPChat, MMDialog, DailyDialog, SODA, MSC, Conversation Chronicles (LoCoMo is ~9x longer per conversation than MSC).
benchmark_family: memory (LoCoMo) - this paper IS the LoCoMo long-term conversational-memory benchmark, a canonical entry in the memory benchmark family alongside LongMemEval. Also touches QA (multi-hop, temporal) and multi-modal dialogue.
baselines: Three model classes on QA: (1) Base short-context LLMs with truncated history: Mistral-Instruct-7B (8K), Llama-2-Chat-70B (4,096), GPT-3.5-turbo (4,096), GPT-4-turbo (4,096); (2) Long-context: GPT-3.5-turbo-16K (context swept 4K/8K/12K/16K); (3) RAG: DRAGON retriever + GPT-3.5-turbo-16K reader over Dialog / Observation / Summary databases at various top-k. Human performance is the upper bound. Event summarization baselines: Mistral-Instruct-7B, Llama-2-Chat-70B, GPT-4-turbo, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-3.5-turbo-16K (incremental summarization; no RAG). Multimodal generation: three MiniGPT-5 variants (Base / +summary / +observation), initialized from a MiniGPT-5 checkpoint fine-tuned on MMDialog.
key_metrics: QA: F1 (partial/exact-match F1 after normalization), per reasoning category and Overall; Recall@k (R@k) for retrieval accuracy of the gold answer-containing context (RAG). Event summarization: FactScore-based Precision/Recall/F1 (atomic-fact decomposition) plus ROUGE-1/2/L. Multi-modal dialogue generation: MM-Relevance plus standard NLG metrics. Human upper bound reported for QA.
headline_result: On LoCoMo QA, all models lag far behind the human F1 of 87.9 Overall. Best base/long-context model GPT-4-turbo (4K) reaches 32.1 Overall; GPT-3.5-turbo-16K (16K) reaches 37.8 Overall. RAG (DRAGON + GPT-3.5-turbo-16K) with top-5 OBSERVATIONS reaches 41.4 Overall F1 (the best configuration), but observation-RAG F1 degrades as k grows beyond 5 (signal-to-noise). Long-context LLMs collapse on adversarial questions (GPT-3.5-turbo-16K adversarial F1 = 2.1 vs 70.2 for 4K GPT-4-turbo). Temporal reasoning is the hardest category (models ~17-26 F1 vs human 92.6). Summarized: long-context/RAG improve memory by 22-66% over base but still lag human by ~56% overall and ~73% on temporal reasoning.
ablations: (1) Context-length sweep for GPT-3.5-turbo-16K (4K/8K/12K/16K): single-hop/multi-hop F1 rise sharply with more context (single-hop 31.7->56.4) but adversarial F1 COLLAPSES (13.1->2.1), showing long context induces hallucination/misattribution. (2) Retrieval-unit ablation (Table 3): Dialog vs Observation vs Summary databases - observations give the best QA F1 (top-5 obs = 41.4 Overall) and especially help temporal (~42) and adversarial (44.7 at top-5); summaries help recall but not F1 (information loss in dialog->summary conversion); raw dialogs improve over no-retrieval but plateau. (3) Top-k sweep: observation-RAG F1 peaks at k=5 and decreases at k=10/25/50 (SNR effect) while Recall@k keeps rising - decoupling recall from answer quality. (4) Event-summarization: long-context GPT-3.5-turbo-16K is WORSE than 4K GPT-3.5-turbo (precision -3.0, recall -8.7), and lags base by ~14%, showing long-context models do not use context well; incremental summarization with GPT-3.5-turbo gives best F1. (5) Multimodal generation: MiniGPT-5 +observation > +summary > Base; MM-Relevance drops as dialog-history length grows, and RAG (observations) partially alleviates the drop. (6) Manual error taxonomy for QA (temporal/open-domain hardest) and 5 event-summary error types (missing info, hallucination, dialog-cue misunderstanding, speaker misattribution, salience errors).
evaluation_decoupling: Yes: intrinsic retrieval quality (Recall@k of the gold answer context) is reported in Table 3 SEPARATELY from end-to-end QA answer-prediction F1. The paper explicitly shows recall and F1 decouple - e.g. summary-RAG attains high recall but low F1, and observation-RAG F1 drops as k (and recall) increases.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Both: outcome metrics are QA F1, summarization FactScore-F1/ROUGE, and MM-Relevance; process/intermediate metrics include retrieval Recall@k (was the right context retrieved), per-reasoning-category breakdown (single/multi/temporal/open-domain/adversarial), and qualitative error taxonomies for QA and event summarization. FactScore decomposes summaries into atomic facts (fine-grained factuality rather than only final overlap).
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Reported as the recall-vs-precision / context-length-vs-accuracy tradeoff rather than wall-clock cost: longer context and larger top-k raise retrieval recall but can hurt QA F1 (SNR), so a small top-k (=5) observation-RAG is both cheaper (fewer/shorter retrieved items) and more accurate than dumping the whole 16K context or top-50. RAG is positioned as a balanced compromise between cheap short-context accuracy and expensive long-context comprehension. No explicit API-cost/latency/token-savings numbers are tabulated. Dataset curation cost is noted (release trimmed 50 -> 10 conversations for cost-effective closed-source evaluation).
context_budget_and_selection_count: Reranked/truncated fixed-k: QA RAG uses top-k retrieved units (k in {5,10,25,50} for dialog/observation; {2,5,10} for summaries), concatenated into the gpt-3.5-turbo-16K reader context. Long-context baselines sweep explicit token budgets 4K/8K/12K/16K; base baselines truncate to 4,096-8K. The best operating point is the small budget top-5 observations, chosen for signal-to-noise rather than maximal recall.
survey_scope_and_axes: N/A (this is a benchmark/dataset paper, not a survey).
benchmark_construction_and_size: Construction: machine-human pipeline. (a) Personas expanded from MSC seeds via gpt-3.5-turbo; (b) per-agent temporal event graph (up to 25 causally-linked events over 6-12 months) generated by text-davinci-003 iteratively (batches of k=3); (c) two generative agents (Park et al. 2023 architecture: reflect-and-respond with long-term observation memory + short-term session summaries) converse, with image-sharing (caption->keywords->icrawler web search) and image-reaction (BLIP-2 caption then react); (d) human annotators edit ~15% of dialog turns, remove/substitute ~19% of images, and verify event-graph grounding. Size: original arXiv v1 = 50 conversations; RELEASED benchmark = 10 conversations (locomo10.json), each ~300 turns / ~9.2K tokens / up to 35 sessions (avg 19.3 sessions, 304.9 turns, 9,209.2 tokens), multi-modal, spanning a few months - ~9x longer per conversation than MSC. Answer verifiability: QA answers are taken verbatim from the conversation where possible and annotated with evidence turn IDs, enabling F1 partial-match and Recall@k scoring; event-summary ground truth = annotated per-speaker event lists scored by FactScore. Difficulty: best system (top-5 observation RAG) ~41.4 QA F1 vs human 87.9; long-context adversarial F1 as low as 2.1, signaling a hard benchmark.
builds_on: Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023) memory/reflection architecture for the dialogue-generating agents; MSC / 'Beyond Goldfish Memory' (Xu et al., 2022) for seed personas and as the prior multi-session benchmark it extends; DRAGON (Lin et al., 2023) as the dense retriever; FactScore (Min et al., 2023) for summarization factuality; MM-Relevance / MMDialog (Feng et al., 2023) and MiniGPT-5 (Zheng et al., 2023) for multimodal dialogue; BLIP-2 (Li et al., 2023b) for image captioning; SODA/Conversation Chronicles (Kim et al. 2023; Jang et al. 2023) for LLM-generated dialogue datasets.
contrasts_with: Prior long-term dialogue benchmarks limited to <=5 sessions / ~1K tokens (MSC - Xu et al. 2022; Conversation Chronicles - Jang et al. 2023; Zhang et al. 2023), and shorter multimodal dialogue datasets (MPChat, MMDialog, DailyDialog, SODA) - LoCoMo is far longer (300 turns, 9K tokens, up to 35 sessions). Methodologically it contrasts long-context LLMs vs RAG vs short-context base LLMs, finding long-context models hallucinate (adversarial collapse, weak event summarization) while distilled-observation RAG is the best balance.
lineage: Surveys/benchmarks group: a foundational very-long-term conversational-MEMORY benchmark (LoCoMo). It established the standard testbed for evaluating long-context vs RAG memory in dialogue agents and is cited as the canonical 'memory' benchmark (alongside LongMemEval) for later agent-memory systems (Mem0, MemGPT, A-MEM, Memory-R1, etc.). Sits in the lineage of multi-session dialogue benchmarks (MSC -> Conversation Chronicles -> LoCoMo) with added scale, multimodality, temporal event-graph grounding, and a three-task evaluation framework.
cbr_cycle_coverage: [Retrieve: yes (dense top-k retrieval of past dialog/observations in the RAG setting), Reuse: partial (retrieved context is reused as prompt evidence to answer, not as a prior solved case), Revise: no, Retain: no (at eval time)]. Not a case-based-reasoning system.
explicit_cbr_grounding: False: the paper does not frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not cite Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner. It is a long-term conversational-memory benchmark with episodic-memory RAG.
tool_document_engineering: N/A: no tools/APIs are retrieved; retrieval is over conversation content (dialogs/observations/summaries).
index_content_separation: Partial / by-construction: the retrievable index is a derived, lighter representation (observations = atomic assertions, or session summaries) separated from the full raw dialog; the reader is then given only the retrieved subset rather than the whole conversation. This is closer to a representation-choice ablation than an explicit progressive-disclosure/index-then-content protocol.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: N/A: no tool index or integration protocol (RapidAPI/REST/MCP/function-calling); retrieval is over a static per-conversation text store.
tool_dependency_awareness: N/A: no inter-tool dependency modeling (no tools).
adaptation_mechanism: N/A (not framed as CBR): retrieved context is used verbatim as in-context evidence for the reader to answer; there is no case-adaptation/revision step.
